opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the internet is a wonderful case study, partly because I lived through it. I was at USC and then Berkeley in the mid-nineties, and we actually put one of the first robots on the web, the Telegarden, where people anywhere in the world could log in and plant seeds and water them with an industrial robot arm. So I got to see that early excitement up close.

What strikes me is that the people who were enthusiastic in the late nineties weren't wrong about where things were going. They were wrong about *when*. There's that line often attributed to Roy Amara: we tend to overestimate the effect of a technology in the short run and underestimate it in the long run. The dot-com era is almost a textbook example. People said everyone would shop online, get their news online, socialize online. All of that happened. But in 1999 most people were on dial-up modems, there was no broadband infrastructure to speak of, no smartphones, and payment systems and logistics weren't ready. So the valuations got way ahead of the underlying capabilities, and in 2000 and 2001 you had the crash. Pets.com became the punchline.

But the crash didn't mean the idea was dead. A lot of the fiber that got laid during the bubble ended up being bought cheaply and became the backbone for what came next. Amazon nearly went under and then became, well, Amazon. So the bust was a kind of correction in expectations, and then the real, slower, more durable growth followed.

The reason I find that so relevant is that I see a very similar dynamic in robotics and AI right now. There's enormous excitement, particularly about humanoid robots, and people are extrapolating from what large language models have done to assume robots will be in every home within a few years. I'm skeptical of that timeline. Language models had the whole internet to train on, but there's no comparable dataset for robot manipulation, and the physical world is just much less forgiving. Grasping an arbitrary object reliably, the thing a two-year-old does effortlessly, is still really hard. I think of it as a "data gap."

So my worry is that if expectations get too far ahead of reality, we could see a bust, a kind of robotics winter, where investors pull back and good research gets defunded. I don't think that would mean robots aren't coming. I'm quite optimistic in the long run. But I think the lesson of the internet is that it's healthier to be honest about the pace, because the long-run payoff is very real, and the hype can actually get in its way.

r001.rationale: It describes the dot-com crash as a correction in expectations, followed by durable growth built on the fiber infrastructure and businesses that survived.

r002.rationale: It says the early predictions about online shopping, news, and socializing all came true, and does not state that the internet’s eventual impact fell short of the boom’s grand expectations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I lived through it, right in the middle of it in the Bay Area, so I have a pretty visceral sense of it. And I think the key thing to understand is that the hype wasn't exactly wrong. People in 1999 were saying the internet was going to transform commerce, transform media, transform how we communicate. And every one of those things turned out to be true. The problem was the timing and the specific bets.

So you had this pattern that Gartner later formalized as the hype cycle: a technology emerges, expectations shoot way past what the technology can actually deliver in the short term, there's a crash of disillusionment, and then there's this long, slow climb where the real value gets built out. Amazon almost didn't survive the crash. Pets.com and Webvan didn't. But the idea behind Webvan, groceries delivered to your door, is now a totally normal thing. It just needed another fifteen years of infrastructure, smartphones, logistics, cheap bandwidth, consumer habits.

I think about this a lot with robotics and AI, because I see the same dynamics. There's an enormous gap between a demo and a deployment. A demo shows you what's possible once, under controlled conditions. Deployment means it works ten thousand times, in the rain, with a part that's slightly out of place. And the people funding these things often can't tell the difference, so money floods in on the demos. Then reality catches up.

What I take from the internet boom is not cynicism. The technology really did change the world. It's more a kind of humility about pace. Most of the big predictions eventually come true, but on a schedule that's much longer and bumpier than anyone selling the vision wants to admit. So when I hear confident timelines, whether it's about robots in every home or fully autonomous everything, my instinct is: the direction is probably right, the date is probably wrong, and some of the companies betting on it will be the Webvans rather than the Amazons.

r001.rationale: The response describes a crash of disillusionment followed by a long climb in which the internet’s real value was built out, with Webvan’s idea becoming normal about fifteen years later.

r002.rationale: The response says the early predictions about the internet’s transformative impact turned out to be true; it emphasizes delays and failed companies, but does not say the internet’s eventual impact fell short of the early expectations.

astra-6.text:
I think the internet boom and bust illustrates a pattern we see with a lot of technologies: the excitement gets ahead of what we can actually deliver. People see something genuinely promising, and then they extrapolate. Suddenly it’s going to change everything, immediately. Investment pours in, expectations rise, and eventually there’s a gap between those expectations and reality.

But the bust doesn’t mean the underlying technology was an illusion. The internet continued to develop. People kept working on the infrastructure and figuring out what it was actually useful for. And over time, it became enormously consequential.

So I think it’s useful to separate the enthusiasm around a technology from the technology itself. You can be skeptical of the promises people are making today and still be optimistic about what sustained work will make possible.

r001.rationale: The response says the internet continued developing after the bust and became consequential over time, but does not clearly state that substantive development emerged years after the hype collapse.

r002.rationale: The response calls the internet enormously consequential and does not say its eventual impact fell short of the grand expectations of the boom.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the internet boom and bust illustrates how easy it is to confuse the potential of a technology with how quickly that potential will be realized. People saw something genuinely important, and then expectations raced ahead of what anyone could actually deliver. There was this sense that everything was going to change overnight.

When that didn’t happen, the reaction swung in the other direction: well, perhaps the whole thing was overblown. But a collapse in expectations isn’t the same as a collapse in the technology. People kept working on it, the infrastructure kept improving, and useful applications continued to emerge.

So I’d distinguish the excitement around a technology from its underlying development. The excitement can rise and fall very rapidly. Getting something to work reliably, and figuring out where it’s actually useful, generally takes much longer.

r001.rationale: The response says useful applications continued to emerge and development took longer, but it does not identify substantive development as emerging years after the hype collapse.

r002.rationale: It says early expectations raced ahead of what could be delivered quickly, but does not state that the internet’s eventual impact fell short of those expectations.
